title: Karna Worships Krishna and Takes His Leave
story:
"Knowing everything, why do you still seek to beguile me?"

Karna had listened to all of Krishna's words, the revelation of his birth, the offer of a kingdom, the plea to change course, and he had worshipped Krishna before he answered, honoring the man who had spoken them. Now he gave his answer, and it was not the answer of a man who could be turned. The destruction of the whole earth was at hand, he said, and its causes were Sakuni, and Dussasana, and king Duryodhana. A great and fierce battle was coming between the Pandavas and the Kurus, a battle that would cover the earth with bloody mire, and all the kings and princes following Duryodhana, consumed by the fire of weapons, would proceed to the abode of Yama.

And then, because he wanted Krishna to understand that he spoke with open eyes, he told him what he had seen. The omens were everywhere, and they all pointed one way. Saturn was afflicting the constellation Rohini; Mars was wheeling toward Jyeshtha and Anuradhas, sign of a great slaughter of friends; the planet Mahapat lay heavy on Chitra. The spot on the moon's disc had shifted, and Rahu approached the sun. Meteors fell from the sky with loud noise and trembling motion. Elephants sent forth frightful cries, while the horses shed tears and refused their food and drink. In every division of Duryodhana's army the soldiers ate little and passed much, a sign the wise called a defect, while the elephants and steeds of the Pandavas were cheerful, and the animals wheeled to their right, an omen of success. The same animals passed to the left of Duryodhana's army, and incorporeal voices were heard over their heads. Auspicious birds, peacocks, swans, cranes, followed the Pandavas, while vultures and kankas and hawks, wolves and bees, followed the Kauravas. The drums in Duryodhana's camp yielded no sound, while the drums of the Pandavas sounded without being struck. The wells in the Kaurava encampment roared like bulls. The gods showered flesh and blood on Duryodhana's soldiers, vapoury edifices with high walls and porches appeared in the sky over their camp, and a black circle surrounded the solar disc. Both twilights were terrible, and the jackals yelled. Birds with one wing, one eye, and one leg cried out in the dark, and fierce birds with black wings and red legs hovered over the camp at nightfall. Duryodhana's soldiers had begun to hate the Brahmanas first, then their preceptors, then their own servants. The eastern horizon was red, the southern the hue of weapons, the western earthy, and all the quarters around the encampment seemed ablaze. "In all these portents," Karna said, "great is the danger that is indicated."

And he had seen more than omens; he had seen a vision. Yudhishthira was ascending with his brothers a palace supported by a thousand columns, all of them in white robes and white head-gear, seated on white seats. Krishna himself was enveloping the blood-dyed earth with weapons. Yudhishthira, of immeasurable energy, stood upon a heap of bones and gladly ate buttered payasa from a golden cup, and he swallowed the earth that Krishna handed to him, which meant that he would rule it. And Bhima, fierce Vrikodara, stood on a summit, mace in hand, devouring the earth, which meant that he would slay them all in battle. Karna recited all of it without flinching, every sign of the ruin of his own side, as a man might recite a verdict already delivered.

Krishna heard him to the end. His answer was short, and it was the most terrible thing Karna would hear that day. "Indeed, the destruction of the earth is at hand," he said, "when my words do not become acceptable to your heart."

Then Karna pressed Krishna to his bosom, holding him once, as a man holds a friend he may never see again. Dismissed by Kesava, he descended from the chariot. The two parted on the road, each knowing what the other knew, each having said everything that could be said, and the earth went on toward its destruction.
reflection: Karna's catalogue of omens is the testimony of a man who sees his own side's ruin and refuses to look away; he does not read the portents as a warning to flee but as a truth to accept. Krishna's reply, that the destruction of the earth is at hand when even his words cannot reach Karna's heart, turns the omens inward: the deepest sign lies not in the sky but in the failure of persuasion.
next_story_tease: Krishna rode on to Upaplavya, where the Pandavas waited for his report.
hero_scene: Karna presses Krishna to his bosom in farewell beside the chariot on the road from Hastinapura, while above them the sky gathers omens, meteors falling and the sun ringed with black.
